p.title: The Effect of Political Advertising after Citizens United: Adjusting for Unmeasured Confounding in Marginal Structural Models

ext.title: Political Advertising after Citizens United: IPTW-FE for MSMs
ext.venue: Metadata hint said "Working paper". The text is a manuscript dated February 9, 2026 with "Comments welcome"; no venue, journal or series is stated.
ext.coverage: Read the entire extracted text file (3,671 lines, 123,945 bytes; the 104,593-char hint was wrong) in four chunks: front matter, Sections 1-7, references, and Appendices A-D including all figure captions and numeric residue. Read all 90 highlights in the single annotation file (559bf8cc8dc4.json). Paul's markup: 90 Highlight annotations, all by Paul Goff, all with empty content, no sticky notes, no dates, and three highlight colours (yellow, green, pink). Covered text is paraphrased, not reproduced, under the copyright rule. Scope check: the paper contains no lobbying-network, path-finding, allocation, or legislator-level content; its only network-adjacent material is the interest-group ad treatment and the cited literature.
ext.research_question: Do independent interest-group TV ads affect Senate and gubernatorial vote shares and turnout after Citizens United, and can an MSM estimator be adjusted for time-constant unmeasured confounding (unit-level heterogeneity) when only a single outcome is observed?
ext.theory: Time-varying treatment with feedback: campaigns and groups respond to each other's ad decisions, so treatment and covariates co-evolve, causing time-varying confounding. Sequential ignorability is a poor fit when groups target markets with persuadable voters by a metric the researcher does not observe (p.3, p.8). The paper proposes a unit-specific sequential ignorability (Assumption 1, p.11): conditional on an unmeasured time-constant alpha_i, treatment is independent of future potential outcomes and covariates. The MSM is a g-computation-style marginal model for treatment histories (pp.8-9, 15).
ext.data: Unit: media market by race (market-race), weekly panel over the campaign window from primary to general election (8 to 40 weeks, median 20; p.25). Races: US Senate and gubernatorial general elections, 2010-2020 (pp.6, 25). Sample after dropping no-treatment-variation races: N = 467 market-races for Democratic IG ads and N = 623 for Republican IG ads (p.25). Sources: Wesleyan Media Project ad data covering all broadcast stations (Fowler et al., 2019); CQ Voting and Elections Collection outcomes; CVAP from US Census; RealClearPolitics polls; county-to-media-market mapping from Sides et al. (2022) (p.6). Simulations (Section 5, p.21): n in {200, 500, 1000, 3000} units, rho = n/T in {5, 10, 50}, 500 Monte Carlo replications (p.23).
ext.method: Proposed IPTW-FE: a two-step procedure. Step 1 fits a parametric logit propensity model with unit-specific fixed effects alpha_i by conditional MLE (incidental-parameters setting). Step 2 builds stabilized inverse-probability weights over the last k+1 periods and solves the weighted MSM estimating equation (weighted least squares for the identity link) (pp.15-17). Theorem 1 gives sqrt(N)-consistency and asymptotic normality with a sandwich variance, with N and T growing at the same rate (p.17); appendix proofs in Appendix A (pp.41-53). Comparators: IPTW with no fixed effects (race-level FE only), and a naive approach that ignores time-varying covariates. Empirical MSM (p.26): E[Y_i(d) | R_i] = gamma_R + gamma_1 * sum_{k=0}^{4} d_{T-k}, race-specific intercepts, effect of one extra week of IG ads in the last five weeks. Weighting model covariates (p.27): lagged Dem poll share and square, undecided/third-party share, Republican negativity over six weeks, cumulative ads by each party and squares, market-race FE. Simulations report bias, SE and 90% CI coverage (pp.22-24).
ext.identification: Unit-specific sequential ignorability (Assumption 1, p.11): conditional on the past treatment history, the covariate history and an unmeasured time-constant alpha_i, treatment is independent of future potential outcomes and future covariates. This allows time-constant measured and unmeasured confounding plus time-varying measured confounding, but rules out time-varying unmeasured confounding (p.12). Positivity is needed. Within-unit treatment switching is required (p.1). A no-anticipation assumption is built into the covariate process (p.11). Truncated MSMs (fixed k lags) are used so the number of propensity parameters, and hence incidental-parameter bias, stays limited (pp.10-11). Identification is not from a pre-period or a difference-in-differences design, because there is one endpoint outcome per unit (p.5, p.4).
ext.scope: Population: US Senate and gubernatorial general-election market-races, 2010-2020, using broadcast TV ads by independent interest groups (ads by candidates and parties are excluded; p.6). Unit of analysis is the media market (not county or state). Era: pre- and post-Citizens United (2010 decision), with a split at Trump's candidacy. Methodological scope: truncated MSMs with a fixed-length treatment history and a fixed-length parameter vector, with N and T growing at the same rate (pp.10, 15). Empirical findings are about down-ballot races and are not generalised to presidential races.

key_findings.finding: Democratic IG ads raise the Democratic share of the two-party vote; the effect is driven by a positive effect on Democratic turnout and a weaker negative effect on Republican turnout (per the text; figure values not extractable).
key_findings.location: Section 6.2, p.28 (Figure 3); Introduction p.4; Abstract p.1
key_findings.numbers: Coefficients appear only in Figure 3; no point estimates in the text. Results significant at alpha=0.1 per p.30.

key_findings.finding: Republican IG ads have no estimated effect on any measured outcome.
key_findings.numbers: No estimate in text; described as null.

key_findings.finding: The effectiveness of Democratic IG ads is concentrated in the post-Trump era (after 2016 per Abstract and p.5; text on p.30 says 2015). Democratic ads more effective at increasing Democratic votes and reducing Republican votes; differences significant at alpha = 0.1.
key_findings.location: Section 6.2, p.30 (Figure 4, pp.29-30); Abstract p.1; p.5
key_findings.numbers: Significance at alpha=0.1; no point estimates in text. Years inconsistent: 2015 (p.30) vs 2016 (p.1, p.5, Figure 4 caption p.29).

key_findings.finding: Democratic IG ads in the last three weeks show a somewhat stronger positive effect than those 4-5 weeks out; the text calls this consistent with prior experiments.
key_findings.numbers: Figure 5 only; no numeric values in text.

key_findings.finding: Magnitudes compared with the literature: Sides et al. (2022) find 0.38-0.87 pp Democratic vote share per 1,000 Democratic-minus-Republican ads; Hewitt et al. (2024) find 1.2-2.3 pp for internal experiments; Klumpp et al. (2016) find 4.1-6.4 pp on House win probability from Citizens United. The authors say their magnitudes are within the broad range and their estimates are slightly higher than Sides et al.
key_findings.numbers: Sides et al.: 0.38-0.87 pp per 1,000 ads; Hewitt et al.: 1.2-2.3 pp; Klumpp et al.: 4.1-6.4 pp House win probability.

key_findings.finding: Placebo tests: IPTW and IPTW-FE estimates on lagged (previous-election) outcomes and pre-election Democratic poll share are close to zero; the naive approach shows residual confounding for some Democratic-ad effects.
key_findings.numbers: Figure 6 only; no numeric values in text.

key_findings.finding: Balance: both IPTW and IPTW-FE sharply reduce conditional imbalance in measured time-varying covariates relative to naive; unweighted data have a few extremely unbalanced time-varying confounders.
key_findings.numbers: Standardized absolute coefficients in Figure 2 only.

key_findings.finding: Positivity violations are common in the last five weeks: Table 1 counts weeks of Democratic IG ads for the final five weeks by year and by number of weeks; the paper's motivation for MSMs rests on this.
key_findings.numbers: Table 1 reports counts by year (2010-2020); not summarised in text.

key_findings.finding: Simulation, low heterogeneity (alpha range [-1,1], FE explain ~1/3 of treatment variance): IPTW-FE bias indistinguishable from IPTW-True; nominal 90% coverage across n and rho; works at n=200, T=4. Naive IPTW has higher bias but smaller SEs.
key_findings.numbers: n in {200,500,1000,3000}; rho in {5,10,50}; 500 MC replications; true effects tau_F=1, tau_C=0.3.

key_findings.finding: Simulation, high heterogeneity (alpha range [-2,2], FE explain ~2/3 of variance): IPTW-FE bias is larger than IPTW-True but shrinks with n and T; naive IPTW bias stays constant as n and T grow; the proposed method still beats naive.

Propensity-score fixed effects are not identified for always- or never-treated units; IPTW-FE can drop them, impute bounded alpha, or use imputed propensity scores (0.01/0.99). Including them with imputed FE (Supplemental D) gives similar results, but naive IPTW is no longer significant for Democratic ads.
key_findings.numbers: Imputed propensity scores 0.01 and 0.99 (p.19); no-variation races dropped in main results.

key_findings.finding: Robustness to propensity-score link misspecification (probit fit to a logit truth) is good: bias and coverage close to correct specification, with slightly higher SEs.
Adding a linear election-year trend interacted with covariates in the weighting model leaves main results similar, with slightly wider uncertainty.

limitations: Assumption 1 is violated by time-varying unmeasured confounding, a limitation the paper shares with linear fixed effects and difference-in-differences (p.12).
With one endpoint outcome per unit, a doubly robust estimator with outcome-regression models is not feasible without strong assumptions (p.19).
Truncated MSMs rule out cumulative full-treatment-history terms; long-term effects cannot be estimated while adjusting for unmeasured confounding (p.11).
Consistency requires a correctly specified parametric propensity model for covariates, plus fixed-length parameter vectors (pp.14-15). The model-specific results are asymptotic.
Finite-sample second-order bias scales with propensity extremity and short T; strong heterogeneity is worse. A jackknife correction is left to future work (pp.18-19).
Positivity: fixed effects are not identified for units never or always treated; the three remedies (omit, impute, bound alpha) each trade bias for variance (pp.19-20).
Residual unmeasured confounding remains a worry the authors acknowledge (p.32), though placebo tests are null (p.33).
The paper assumes no interference across media markets (p.6) and treats ads as weeks of presence, not ad counts; the comparison with Sides et al. is therefore indirect (p.32).
Only broadcast television ads are measured; the approach uses the market-race as the unit, and county outcomes are mapped to markets (p.6).

Simulation evidence uses 500 MC replications and only the correctly specified MSM in the main text; the proposed estimator is slightly biased under high heterogeneity even with the true propensity score (p.24).
Internal inconsistency: the Trump-candidacy split is dated 2015 on p.30 but 2016 in the Abstract (p.1), p.5 and the Figure 4 caption (p.29).
Metadata inconsistency to note: the text does not state a venue; the title and authors match the hint.
measures: Outcomes (p.6): Democratic share of the two-party vote (CQ returns); Democratic turnout % (Dem votes / CVAP); Republican turnout % (Rep votes / CVAP); placebo outcomes: lagged two-party vote, lagged Dem and Rep turnout from the previous election for the same office, and pre-election Democratic poll share.

Treatment (p.6): binary D_it = 1 if an independent group (any interest or advocacy group other than candidate or party, including dark-money groups and PACs) ran TV ads in market i in week t; separate analyses for Democratic and Republican groups; cumulative weeks in last five weeks of campaign.

Covariates (p.27): average Democratic poll share in previous week and its square; average undecided or third-party share; Republican negativity (attack ads) over last six weeks; cumulative ads shown by Democrat and Republican and squares; attack-ad coding from Wesleyan data (p.6).
Simulation measures (pp.22-23): bias, standard error (HC2 sandwich), and 90% CI coverage for tau_F and tau_C.

rel.summary_md:
Blackwell and Yamauchi (manuscript, 9 Feb 2026) ask whether TV ads run by independent interest groups after Citizens United changed vote shares and turnout. The sample is US Senate and gubernatorial general elections, 2010-2020, measured as weekly media-market by race panels (N = 467 market-races for Democratic-group ads, 623 for Republican). The methods problem is feedback: ads and campaign conditions shape each other, and groups may target persuadable markets on information the researcher cannot see. The authors fit a propensity model with a fixed effect for each unit (estimated by conditional MLE) and use it to build inverse-probability weights for a truncated marginal structural model. They prove root-N consistency when N and T grow together. In simulations (500 replications) the estimator beats IPTW without fixed effects, although some bias remains when heterogeneity is high.

Empirically, Democratic-group ads raise the Democratic two-party share, mostly by raising Democratic turnout, and the effect is concentrated after Trump's candidacy. Republican-group ads show no effect. Placebo tests on lagged outcomes come out near zero. Effects are significant only at alpha 0.1, the text gives no point estimates, and the Trump split is dated 2015 on p.30 but 2016 elsewhere.

For Paul's systems this is mainly a methods paper. It sharpens the caution on Mentat's fixed-effects regressions of sector growth on spending, and it shows a placebo-outcome check that the prospective receptivity contract lacks. It also gives one weak, party-asymmetric data point on Terrier's split between persuasion and mobilization. It says nothing about legislators, so it cannot support the competitiveness multiplier or any part of the flip model's money terms.

bearings.paper_claim: Unit fixed-effects regressions are biased when treatment and time-varying covariates feed back on each other (citing Imai & Kim 2019 and Sobel 2012). The paper's remedy moves the fixed effects into a propensity model and requires a binary treatment that switches within units, a correctly specified parametric propensity model, and N and T growing together. Simulations use n of 200-3000 with T of at least 4; in the empirical panel, campaign windows run 8-40 weeks.
bearings.system_side: Fits OLS of log giving and log lobbying on sector FE, growth, phase, tossup and trend, with variants that add year FE (variant year_fe) and a lagged/AR lobbying term, using wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector. Brain record: the L3-LV coefficient +0.352 becomes -0.477 with sector+year FE, and the first-difference lead is -0.537 over 71 pairs.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the diagnosis transfers, not the estimator. The study's 'treatment' is continuous sector growth with few sector clusters and annual T, so IPTW-FE cannot run: there is no binary switching treatment and no feasible propensity model. Read the paper as support for the study's existing choice to keep the lobbying-lead results DESCRIPTIVE. A sign flip under added FE is what feedback or time-varying confounding produces, so neither sign is causal. Carries over to any sector-year panel in which lagged lobbying or giving enters as a regressor.

bearings.paper_claim: Placebo tests check the identifying assumptions by applying the estimator to outcomes measured before treatment: the previous election's vote share and turnout, and the pre-election poll share. IPTW-FE estimates are near zero, while the naive approach shows residual confounding for some Democratic-ad effects.
bearings.system_side: H1 is a Spearman correlation between the frozen seed_prob and new cosponsorships after the freeze. H2 is a Spearman correlation between pressure_mult and absolute tier movement. Both are cross-sectional, with no pre-freeze placebo. The contract requires at least 60 days and 150 movers, and returns UNDERPOWERED without consuming the look.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The placebo logic carries over directly. A pre-registered negative control would be Spearman(seed_prob, cosponsorship delta over a window that ends before the freeze). A non-zero value would show that seed_prob tracks a stable member trait (a time-constant confounder) rather than responsiveness. Adding it changes the contract, so it needs Paul's ruling before the single look is spent, and it needs a second pre-freeze snapshot pair. Neither H1 nor H2 measures a lobbying treatment, so even a PASS remains an association.

bearings.paper_claim: Democratic interest-group TV ads raise the Democratic two-party share mainly by raising Democratic turnout, with a weaker negative effect on Republican turnout. Republican interest-group ads have no estimated effect on any outcome. The Democratic effect is concentrated after Trump's candidacy and is significant at alpha 0.1. No point estimates are given in the text.
bearings.system_side: potential = (wp x (1-|2s-1|) x t + (1-wp) x s x (1-t)) x (1 + wi x i). The weights on persuasion of undecided likely voters and on mobilization of supporters unlikely to vote are symmetric across parties, with default wp 0.5.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The treatment is broadcast TV ads aggregated to the media market in Senate and gubernatorial races, 2010-2020. It is not door-to-door contact, and the outcome is not individual. The finding suggests that mobilization effects can dominate and can differ by party and era, so a fixed, party-symmetric wp is a judgment call that this paper neither validates nor sets. It does not transfer to US House districts (OR-05, CT-01) or to canvassing without field-experiment evidence.

bearings.paper_claim: Groups may target markets with more persuadable voters using a metric the researcher cannot see, so a naive comparison of treated and untreated units is confounded. The paper handles only time-constant unmeasured confounding, through unit fixed effects in the propensity score. Time-varying unmeasured confounding still breaks identification.
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0 x exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0) scales effective dollars on both money legs. AMPLITUDE and SCALE are Paul's judgment constants, uncalibrated, and the reciprocity they encode is explicitly NOT validated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: No direct transfer. The paper estimates effects of ads on voters, not the responsiveness of legislators to PAC dollars, and it must not be cited as support for c (D-104..D-108). Its only bearing is on calibration: any future attempt to estimate c from observed giving and alignment must handle strategic targeting of competitive seats, because givers pick those seats on information the analyst lacks.

gaps_exposed: No component estimates a causal effect of money, ads or lobbying. Every money-response constant in the influence engine (WM/WP, HALFF, MAXSHIFT, COMPET_MULT amplitude and scale) is judgment. The paper shows the kind of design (weekly treatment panel, propensity weighting with unit fixed effects, placebo outcomes) that estimating them would need.
The prospective receptivity contract (H1/H2) has no negative-control or placebo look on pre-freeze outcomes, so it cannot tell responsiveness apart from a stable member trait.

The sector-growth regressions have no design that addresses feedback between lagged lobbying or giving and later covariates. The sign flips under year FE are reported but cannot be interpreted causally.

Neither Mentat nor Melange measures voter-facing outside spending as a treatment with timing. Mentat's transfer graph splits independent-expenditure dollars into support and oppose (89% oppose) but carries no week-level timing or outcome link.
Terrier's persuasion/mobilization weight wp is symmetric and fixed. No evidence base, including this paper, sets it by party or era.
flags: Voter-level evidence only. It must not be quoted as support for the competitiveness multiplier's reciprocity or for any legislator money response; reciprocity is NOT validated (D-104..D-108).

Pooled versus stratified: the Democratic-ad effect is concentrated after Trump's candidacy. Quote the pooled Democratic effect only with the era strata, or label it UNSTRATIFIED. Window: Senate and gubernatorial races 2010-2020; denominators N = 467 (Democratic-group ads) and 623 (Republican-group ads) market-races.
Internal inconsistency: the Trump-era split is dated 2015 on p.30 but 2016 in the Abstract, on p.5 and in the Figure 4 caption.
Results are significant only at alpha 0.1, and the text gives no point estimates (figures only). Do not invent magnitudes.
Any IPTW-FE-style re-analysis of Paul's data by an agent stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal, and it does not use LDA.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul records no takeaways. Both bibliography entries (folder Causal & Methodological, and a5b9f5a95891) are bare citations, which fits his component note that the Causal & Methodological folder is unannotated. His 90 highlights fall almost entirely on method: fixed effects inside the propensity score, the single-outcome setting, the need for treatment switching, the positivity remedies (drop, bound or impute alpha), the simulation design, and three pink conclusion highlights. That suggests he values the paper as an estimation template, not for its findings about ads. The bearings above agree with that reading. The paper's contribution is the confounding diagnosis and the placebo practice, both of which the system's validation discipline could absorb. No note of his is stale relative to the system, because none links this paper to a component.

related.why: Both papers question unit and two-way fixed-effects designs under feedback. Blackwell & Yamauchi cite the 2019 Imai & Kim paper on the same problem. Together they underwrite reading the sector-growth year-FE sign flip as non-causal.
Weimer uses Monte Carlo as a negative control. Blackwell & Yamauchi use placebo outcomes from before treatment. Both are falsification checks that the prospective contract lacks.

Both papers bear on campaign persuasion and its returns, and Broockman co-authored the Hewitt et al. (2024) experiments used here as a magnitude benchmark (1.2-2.3 pp). Together they inform Terrier's split between persuasion and mobilization.

Kalla's experiment identifies the effect of money on legislators' access. This paper identifies the effect of outside spending on voters. The flip model's money assumptions need evidence of the first kind, which this paper does not supply.
